title: His 1979 operation and stay in the Veterans Hospital
summary: Whaley recalls blood in his bladder, an operation and hernia, two months in the Veterans Hospital and rough nurses before his nephew took him home.

story.theme_name: Illness, injury and the deaths of colleagues
story.community_name: Illness, injury and death among jazz musicians

blocks.x: This is December 2, 1979. This is a continuation of an interview with you, Tom Whaley. And how long ago was it since we had the last interview with you?
About six months, isn't it?
It's been about six months. And when I left you got a little ill. Tell me what happened to you?
What do you mean, my operation?
Yeah, yeah.
Oh, I had blood in my bladder, see. And I didn't know it and I went to the hospital on a Tuesday.
How did you happen to find out you had it in there?
You told me.
Right.

Because I know I had a little burning sensation in there and then you told me there was blood. So I went to the hospital on a Tuesday, and the man says, you've got to stay in here. So then my -- Mike, Ruth Ellington's son, he took all my clothes up to the house and I told her to have them cleaned and when I come out I'm going to get it, see.

And I had a money belt and I had $200 in there and I told her about it. So I stayed in the hospital there, a week, I think before they operated on me. And while they were -- they did one operation, then I had a hernia and they -- I think it was double, I'm not sure. But, anyway, they took one out anyway and I recuperated.
I was in the hospital for two months, over two months, see. When I come out in June and my nephew brought me my clothes back. I put them on. Shall I tell you about the
Yeah, sure.
Oh, they were rough, those nurses.
They have to be rough to get you straight. They got you walking, haven't they?
They really turn you -- "stand up". I say, wait a minute.
This is like the Army.
Yeah, this is the Veterans Hospital. They had no mercy at all. But, anyway, I got better, and --
It's not that they don't have any mercy, Tom. They can't cater to your illnesses, they want to get you up. So they have to do it along the lines of militarily.

Yeah. Then the lady that was in charge of getting me out of there, see, -- and my nephew was supposed to come and get me. And it was a mixup there, he didn't come til about 7:00 at night. And he come and he got me home.
Well, that's good. I'm glad you're home.
I'm glad to get home.
